document.title: Comments of Natural Resources Defense Council in response to FERC's 02/20/2025 Order and PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.'s 03/24/2025 Answer

pages.text:
2 
 
 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
In most aspects, NRDC agrees with the conclusions in the PJM Answer: the jurisdictional 
framework suggested by the Commission in the Order is correct; co-located loads’ use of the 
transmission system and wholesale services is a function of the specific configuration; co-located 
loads are best addressed by fitting them into existing market structures.  However, in some areas 
PJM’s Answer appears to suggest unduly preferential treatment for co-located loads or their 
associated generation, and the Answer also misses several specific issues that if left unaddressed 
could lead to unjust cost shifting or reliability violations. 
II. 
COMMENTS 
A. 
Co-Located Load Remains Retail Load and is Unambiguously Under State 
Jurisdiction 
We join OPSI in requesting the Commission affirm that the sale between co-located load 
and the generator is a retail sale subject to state jurisdiction.4 We agree with the Commission’s 
statement in the Order that: 
[U]nder the FPA, the states get to determine which entities are 
legally permitted to provide electricity to retail customers in co-
location arrangements. The states also get to determine how the 
wholesale costs of providing electricity to those retail customers are 
 
4 Post-Technical Conference Comments of the Organization of PJM States, Inc., Docket No. AD24-11-000, at 4 
(Dec. 9, 2024), Accession No. 20241209-5086; see also Comments of the Organization of PJM States, Inc., Docket 
Nos. EL25-49-000 et. al., at 5 (April 23, 2025), Accession No. 20250423-5159. Certain aspects of PURPA 
Qualifying Facilities (18 C.F.R. § 292) are subject to federal regulation, which would extend to co-located 
generation that is also a Qualifying Facility.

3 
 
recovered through retail rates. That is true irrespective of where the 
load interconnects…5 
PJM’s Answer presents several examples where state law does not regulate co-located 
loads.6 None of these call the basic premises above into question, as they all represent cases 
where states have chosen not to exercise authority—in none of them is there any indication that a 
state legislature could not opt to exercise jurisdiction should they choose. While PJM correctly 
points out that there may be places states currently decline to exercise their authority, that does 
not alter the bright line boundary of FERC jurisdiction as set out in the Order. 
B. 
Certain Proposals in the PJM Answer Would Result in Unduly Preferential 
Treatment 
1. 
Creating an expedited interconnection process for generation dedicated to 
co-located loads is unduly discriminatory. 
The PJM Answer proposes one option in which co-located load elects to be network load 
and bring its own generation—either in the form of new generation or arrangements with 
existing generation that has or is scheduled to deactivate. PJM envisions that one way this option 
could be facilitated is through “a potentially faster interconnection path for generation resources 
supporting co-located loads.”7 This would entail a further erosion of open access principles 
beyond those recently approved by FERC as the Reliability Resource Initiative (“RRI”). 
In their concurrence to the RRI Order, Commissioners Phillips and Rosner noted that 
they accepted RRI because “it is a one-time, extraordinary measure.”8 If FERC were to approve 
 
5 Order at P 69. 
6 PJM Answer at 27-29 
7 PJM Answer at 17. 
8 Order Accepting Tariff Revisions re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084, (February 11, 2025) 
(Rosner and Phillips, Comm’rs, concurring at P 1) (“RRI Order”).

4 
 
expedited interconnection for the purposes of serving co-located loads, it would be abandoning 
that bright line for waiving FERC’s “longstanding principle of nondiscriminatory open access,” 
risking “seriously undermin[ing] confidence in Commission-jurisdictional electricity markets.”9 
Rather than a one-time exception in response to an extraordinary reliability issue, special 
treatment of generation serving co-located load would be a routine process that is predicated on a 
determination of which load additions justify special treatment for associated generation. This 
would place PJM and the Commission in the position of deciding what types of load growth 
enjoy priority access to the transmission system. This would potentially put FERC in the middle 
of state decisions on issues such as electrification or data center development. For these reasons, 
the Commission should be deeply skeptical of any proposal along these lines. 
It may be that PJM’s goals could be reached through enhancements to provisional 
interconnection service, as PJM acknowledges.10 If carefully designed, such an approach might 
be non-discriminatory. However, it would require tailored rules to ensure that all generation 
receives the same opportunities to serve load while under provisional interconnection. We 
submit that allowing such arrangements based solely on the existence of an arrangement between 
the generator and a load or load serving entity would be unduly discriminatory, as it would 
contradict many years’ precedent supporting equal access for merchant and utility-affiliated 
generation. Most likely, a non-discriminatory solution would require wide-ranging changes to 
PJM’s deliverability requirements for capacity resources. 
 
9 Concurrence of Commissioners Rosner and Phillips, in 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211, P 6. 
10 PJM Answer at 17.

5 
 
2. 
To avoid undue discrimination, flexibility of co-located loads must be 
treated on the same terms as any other demand response. 
Recent work has highlighted that flexibility on the part of large loads can dramatically 
reduce their impact on system reliability.11 Reflecting this, the PJM Answer includes an option 
for a new non-capacity backed service offering.12 Essentially, PJM proposes offering 
interruptible service to co-located loads. 
However, PJM already has an interruptible service offering, in the form of its existing 
and well-developed demand response rules. Demand response in PJM’s capacity market is, at its 
core, a mechanism for customers to specify the price at which they are willing to designate a 
portion of their load as interruptible, along with detailed provisions for measuring and enforcing 
compliance with commitments to take interruptible service. PJM also offers a little-used Price 
Responsive Demand product that enables load serving entities to reduce their capacity 
obligations to reflect load that is automatically curtailed based on market conditions.13 
The proposed non-capacity backed service would simply be a new third type of demand 
response. That is a perilous path, as it would be difficult to design such a product that did not 
amount to being simply an unduly preferential method for favored loads to provide demand 
response. For example, most load resources in PJM cannot offset their full capacity charge even 
if they commit to dropping to zero consumption on request,14 but PJM’s proposed non-capacity 
 
11 Norris, Tyler, Timothy Profeta, Dalia Patino-Echeverri and Adam Cowie-Haskell, Rethinking Load Growth: 
Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems, (2025). Available at 
https://hdl.handle.net/10161/32077.  
12 PJM Answer at 18. 
13 See PJM Manual 18: PJM Capacity Market, Section 4.3 (demand response) and Section 3A (Price Responsive 
Demand), available at https://www.pjm.com/pjmfiles/directory/manuals/m18/index.html#about.html 
14 Demand Response winter capacity values are determined using a separate baseline from the load’s capacity 
obligation, so a resource can only offset its winter capacity charges if its winter consumption is higher than its 
summer coincident peak hour consumption. See PJM Manual 19: Load Forecasting and Analysis, Attachment A, 
available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m19.pdf

6 
 
service would allow just that. Even if the product was designed to be non-discriminatory, adding 
a new demand response method would require maintenance of a parallel set of market rules. If 
the history of demand response is any indication, it would likely take several iterations over 
many years before all the kinks were worked out of such a product. In the best case, it would 
cause redundant and error-prone work to maintain rules that duplicate existing demand response 
products. 
The region would be much better served by allowing co-located loads to represent their 
flexibility through the existing demand response products. If shortcomings are identified in those 
products that prevent realization of the full value of co-located load flexibility, they should be 
remedied in the existing products so that all flexible load has non-discriminatory opportunity to 
avoid capacity costs. 
PJM’s discussion of this option reveals shortcomings in how demand response is treated 
in planning. Currently, PJM’s transmission planning simply assumes that the amount of demand 
response on the system will remain constant. Straightforward improvements to this unreasonable 
assumption would be appropriate and potentially avoid large unnecessary costs. Currently, 
utilities notify PJM of expected future large loads, which PJM then treats as adjustments to load 
forecasts. There seems to be no barrier to allowing the utilities, or the loads themselves, to also 
provide PJM with information about the future loads’ demand response capability as part of this 
same process. That would enable PJM’s planning to properly consider benefits from load 
flexibility, realizing the same value as the proposed non-capacity backed service without creating 
a new product.

7 
 
C. 
The PJM Answer Fails to Address Important Planning and Reliability Issues 
1. 
Co-located loads that rely on the wholesale grid for backup create a need 
for capacity that is not adequately captured under PJM’s Tariff. 
The PJM Answer presents options where a co-located, non-network load is primarily 
served by its own generator but may draw upon PJM when needed.15 Under current rules, such 
load would generally have no capacity obligation, provided that the on-site generation was 
running during the coincident peak hours PJM uses to allocate capacity costs. If done at scale 
this will create a reliability gap: when the co-located load’s generator is off-line, PJM will have 
load that it has not procured capacity for. Should this occur during a time of system stress, 
reliability may be threatened. This is a matter of particular concern because of the prominence of 
correlated or common-mode generator outages in recent reliability events. If outages of the 
generator serving the co-located load are correlated with outages of PJM’s fleet generally, PJM 
runs a risk of seeing an unplanned for increase in load just when supply is falling short. 
It is well established that utilities may charge for on-demand backup power service.16 
However, PJM’s tariff currently contains no provisions for this. To maintain reliability, capacity 
must be procured for any significant load with the possibility of withdrawing from PJM’s grid 
during emergencies, such as would occur for a co-located load if the associated generator fails.  
Large loads that use backup generators may be somewhat similarly situated to co-located 
loads in this respect, provided that they use their generators to reduce load during coincident 
peaks. In this case, capacity is procured for those loads,17 but the peak shaving load is not 
allocated a share of capacity costs. Since PJM procures capacity based on these loads’ full year 
 
15 Option 5 and Option 4 in the case where the proception system fails. See PJM Answer at 13-15. 
16 See, e.g., 18 CFR § 292.305(b)(ii). 
17 PJM’s IRM requirements are determined based on full load history, not only coincident peaks.

8 
 
consumption profile, but only bills them based on their reduced consumption during coincident 
peak hours, this shifts costs from the peak shaver to other customers. While this is a long-
standing practice, the cost shifts will become significantly larger if data centers interconnect and 
peak shave at the scale currently envisioned.  
Following PJM’s shift to marginal ELCC accreditation,18 PJM’s coincident-peak based 
cost allocation became largely untethered to actual cost causation. Because of changing system 
conditions, peak risk hours, and thus the drivers of the need for capacity, are no longer the hours 
of peak load. At the time, the Commission declined to address that issue. As large loads with the 
ability to peak shave grow, the unintended cost shifts resulting from not updating the capacity 
cost allocation method to match cost causation will grow. 
2. 
Costs incurred on the basis of utility speculation of future loads may not 
be allocated to other utilities. 
 This Section 206 proceeding raises very important issues, but NRDC also urges the 
Commission to be proactive in addressing the other ways in which PJM’s tariff and planning 
procedures need to be updated to the reflect the marked load growth—predominantly driven by 
data center development—currently being experienced across its footprint. Specifically, PJM 
should explore increasing the certainty and discipline in its load forecasting methodologies with 
respect to new large loads. Accurate load forecasts are essential to inform PJM’s transmission 
planning, interconnection procedures, and investment decisions by existing and new generation, 
storage, and demand response resources. Inflated load forecasts could drive a potential costly 
overbuild of the system that would ultimately be paid for by other rate classes other than these 
 
18 Order Accepting Tariff Revisions, 186 FERC ¶ 61,080 (February 11, 2024).

9 
 
large new loads. Many utilities within PJM have already either proposed or finalized tariffs via 
state utility commission proceedings that require large loads above a certain MW threshold to 
provide a significant financial commitment upfront to its load serving entity or electric 
distribution company in order to be included in their respective load forecasts.19 PJM’s load 
forecast methodology should distinguish between large load adjustments that are backed by 
significant financial commitments from those that are not; including only the former in load 
forecasts will minimize the impact of speculative data center projects on consumers, and improve 
transmission and resource planning.   We urge the Commission to examine the extent to which 
RTO load forecasts apply appropriate rigor to exclude speculative data center projects, through 
the Commission’s recently opened AD25-7 proceeding on Meeting the Challenge of Resource 
Adequacy in Regional Transmission Organization and Independent System Operator Regions, 
and other venues.  
 
 
 
19 There are many examples of this approach, including the Indiana Michigan Power Large Load Settlement 
(February 2025), available at https://www.indianamichiganpower.com/company/news/view?releaseID=10036; an 
AEP Ohio tariff filing (May 2024), available at https://www.aepohio.com/company/news/view?releaseID=9539; an 
Appalachian Company tariff filing (March 2025), available at  
https://www.scc.virginia.gov/docketsearch/DOCS/84hh01!.PDF; and a filing by Dominion available at 
https://www.scc.virginia.gov/docketsearch/DOCS/84sc01!.PDF.

10 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
NRDC respectfully requests the Commission consider these comments in determining 
what reforms to PJM rules are necessary to accommodate co-location and large loads.  NRDC 
specifically emphasizes the importance of avoiding special treatment in regards to 
interconnection, demand response opportunities, and planning. 
 
DATED April 23, 2025 
Respectfully submitted,
